chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 4 of 6): the poet confesses bondage to courtesans who lure, rob and expel, the decay of the old body and Death's coming, and his own trade as a poet who praises patrons for gifts and prides himself on titles; he asks for the feet, the six-letter name and the gift of song, and the praise turns on Rama and Vishnu as uncle, Siva burning Kama, and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (66, 67, 73, 74, 77, 78, 79, 80); the aged and dying body (68, 72, 75); the poet's own art misused or made a source of pride (69, 71, 76); and 70, a song on the body of nine gates and the wish to recite the books of knowledge.

66.reading: The poet describes the women who lure men from the street, shaking their breasts and laughing, who set their minds on rich men, take them up to the upper floor, lie with them by lamplight and coax coins from them, demand more as owed, strip even the jewels from their hands, and drive them out exhausted; he asks to be kept from their company. The praise names Vishnu, who in anger struck down the demon of twenty mountain-like arms and ten heads, as the loving uncle, and calls Murugan the Guha of Senthil who also lives in glory at Thiruttani, where fish leap over the field ridges onto heaped pearls.
66.nuance: The sequence is a small drama of the courtesan's house: the street, the upstairs room, the lamp, the coaxing (பசப்பி), the claim 'this is owed for that' (இதுக்கு அதுக்குக் கடப்படாம்), and the expulsion (இளைக்க விட்டுத் துரத்துவார்). A Senthil song names Thiruttani in its last lines (திருத்தணிக்குள் சிறப்பில் வாழ்) before ending at Senthil. The phrase பண்டைகூளமென வாழ் and the closing epithet வயத்த நித்தத் துவத்தனே are hard to divide.

67.reading: The poet speaks of women who draw men to the bed of burning pleasure, gather the gold and ornaments they bring, and when a man is spent tell him to go today; he asks that his mind, which goes so sweetly to them, be given love for Murugan's feet and the power to praise him in poetry and song. The praise recalls Kama, whose arrows made even great ascetics wilt, falling into the fire of Siva who burned him with a slight thought, and the vel that removes the gods' distress, at Senthil where striped bees hum his praise.
67.nuance: அற்றனை என இன்று ஓட்டு என்று: the woman's dismissal once the man has nothing left, the same charge as in 33 and 66. The plea is to redirect the same mind (இனிமையில் ஒன்றாய்ச் சென்று உட்படு மனம்) rather than to kill it. The dense rhythm makes the first eight lines and the phrase திடமுறு அன்பால் சிந்தைக்கு அறிவிடமும் சேர்த்து hard to divide.

68.reading: The poet pictures his old age, belly sagging, hair white, teeth loose, back bent, lips hanging, one hand on a stick, while women laugh 'who is this worn-out old man', his cough rattles, speech slurs, eyes go blind and ears deaf; a physician comes, his young sons ask about property and debts, his wife weeps and falls, and Yama's servants stand by as his filth flows: at that hour, he asks, come quickly on the peacock. The praise is a long lullaby of Kausalya calling the child Rama, 'come, my father, come, lord of the Raghus, come, my son, my eye, my life, come and drink at the breast, come and wear flowers', and calls Murugan the nephew who delights that Mayan's heart, Valli's lover and son of Siva who wears the moon, the serpent and the river, at Senthil.
68.nuance: தொண்டு கிழவன் here means a decrepit old man, not a servant: the same word the book uses for service is turned into mockery in the women's mouths. The deathbed is social as well as bodily: the doctor, the sons asking உடைமை கடன் ஏது, the falling wife. The Kausalya passage, ten repetitions of வருக, mirrors the plea: the poet calls the Lord to come as Kausalya called her child.

69.reading: The poet confesses that, trusting this hut thatched with skin and full of women's deceitful play, he ran after wealth composing new தூது, நான்மணிமாலை, கோவை, உலா and மடல் poems and entering the doors of worthless patrons, and calls himself idle, unjust, a liar and slanderer, shameless, cruel, miserly and reviled; he asks whether grace will not grant a little of the stainless sea of true knowledge and austerity, so that all the sorrow of the world of cause and effect ends. The praise tells of Rama, borne on Hanuman's shoulders, who cut off Ravana's heads and gave Vibhishana his kingdom, and of Narada coming to say 'this is the field where she lives', so that Murugan went to Valli, at Seeralaivay.
69.nuance: The plea names the prabandha genres the poet used to win gifts (தூது, நான்மணிமாலைப் பிரபந்தக் கோவை, உலா, மடல்) and the doors of patrons (தோமுறு காளையர் வாசல்தொறும்): the confession is of poetry sold, not only of lust. தோலொடு மூடிய கூரை, a roof covered with skin, is the body. Narada's part in the Valli story is named outright (நாரதர் வந்துற்று ஈது அவள் வாழ் புனமாம்).

70.reading: The poet speaks of the body of four and five gates, a bush of sinew and bone with arms and legs, in which sound joins at the first gate and its plays go on unnoticed, and asks that before it grows old in seeking endless books and speaking clever words to men he be given a life of reciting fully the books of knowledge in which Murugan is mingled. The praise names the primal one who cried 'refuge' when Death came casting his noose for the boy's life, the silent dark-throated one who looked at Kama and his five arrows and said 'burn', to whom Murugan spoke the Veda, and Vishnu with the discus who ended the elephant's fear, at Senthil where the Vedas seek the feet.
70.nuance: நாலும் ஐந்து வாசல் is the body of nine openings. The plea sets two kinds of learning against each other: the endless books sought with delusion and the clever words that breed harm, and the ஞான நூல் in which the Lord is present. The boy whose life Death came for, with the cry ஓலம், points to the story of Markandeya; whose the cry is, the boy's or Siva's, depends on the division. Several phrases (நாரி என்பில் ஆகும், நாதம் ஒன்ற ஆதி வாயில்) are uncertain.

71.reading: The poet confesses that he compared men to Kubera for wealth, Indra for rank and Kandan for beauty, cried to them that they were his refuge in his great hunger, and sang new verses daily while pouring out his distress; he asks Murugan to break the agitation of the senses in which the body perishes and give him love that unites him to his feet. The praise names Siva, who laughed and burned the strong cities and dances in the hall with the axe, to whom Murugan gave a Tamil verse in rhythm, the splitter of the hill at Senthil, and Murugan who joined his red hands and bowed to the golden creeper of the hunters in the field.
71.nuance: The begging poet even compares patrons to Kandan (நிறத்திற் கந்தன்), the god he should be praising: the flattery borrows Murugan's own name. In the praise Murugan bows to Valli (செங்கரம் குவித்துக் கும்பிடும்), the lover humbling himself. மழுக்கைக் கொண்ட சங்கரர்க்குச் சென்று வண்டமிழ்ச் சொல் சந்தம் ஒன்று அருள்வோனே: the teaching to Siva is given here as Tamil verse.

72.reading: The poet confesses that, taking impermanent things for himself, he wasted long days until his strength went, he grew deaf and blind, full of disease, his senses faltering, swollen on a bed of filth and water, on the way to the burning ground, and asks for the lotus feet that spread as a light the Vedas cannot praise. The praise names the boiling vel that dried the sea like a pond and split the old mango tree of the demons, and calls Murugan the Kumara of Alaivay who showed the highest meaning to Siva of undying pure form, easy for his devotees to reach.
72.nuance: நிலையாப் பொருளை உடலாக் கருதி: the error is taking the passing thing for oneself, and the decay that follows is its result. மறைபோற்ற அரிய ஒளியாய்ப் பரவு மலர்த்தாள் makes the feet a pervading light. The mango tree (சூதம்) is Sura's last form. அடியார்க்கு எளிய: the Lord is easy of access for devotees, the closing note. மடுவேற்கு உரிய நெறியாக is obscure.

73.reading: The poet describes women who make love-pellets ground with sugarcane juice and feed them to men, rub on many scents, hide something inside the betel they give on the bed, then complain 'you never think of me', and so drag men into the net of desire; he asks not to wander in their ways but to be granted daily vision in his heart of the fragrant six letters, the kadamba garland and the radiance of Murugan's face. The praise names Siva of the dark throat and Rama of the bow as kin, lists the shrines where Murugan dwells (Sikkal, Valanchuzhi, Thiruchengodu, Idaikkazhi, Thandalai, Kalar, Chengadu, Kurukkai, Purambayam and others), and the vel that pierced the chest of the deceitful Sura and drank his life, at Thiruchendur.
73.nuance: The deceit named here is the love-charm: கருப்பஞ் சாறொடு அரைத்துள உண்டைகள் and something hidden in the betel (வெற்றிலையின் புறம் ஒளித்து), the courtesans' magic rather than their price. ஆறெனும் அக்கரம், the six letters, is Murugan's six-syllable mantra, set against those potions. The list of shrines in the praise is unusual. The opening phrase நிறுக்கும் சூதன மெய்த்தன முண்டைகள் is hard to divide.

74.reading: The poet asks that, stumbling in the darkness of defiled birth and its bonds, wounded by Kama's five arrows, he not waste away in doubt and delusion in the embraces of deceitful, showy common women, but be given Murugan's flower feet with anklets and bells, and his love. The praise names the vel that broke the demon's power and gave the world back to Indra, a picture of Siva's red matted hair with the moon, konrai, datura and tulasi, and Murugan of fine Tamil at Senthil, where the southern breeze blows through the groves.
74.nuance: பிறப்பு அந்தகாரம், the darkness of birth, and பந்த பாசம, the binding bonds, set the women within the larger bondage of birth. Tulasi (துழாய்), Vishnu's plant, appears among the flowers in Siva's hair; what the peacock (தோகை) in that hair stands for is unclear to me.

75.reading: The poet draws Yama in full, with the five great sins, crescent fangs, fiery hair, poisoned eyes, trident and noose, black as a rain cloud on his graceless buffalo, and asks that at the hour of his coming Murugan come before him, his servant who praises the feet with a love received from generation to generation, on the peacock whose dance cracks the cosmic sphere and shakes the eight directions. The praise dwells on Valli's beauty, her cloud of hair, nectar speech and moonlit smile, with Murugan as the bridegroom asleep on her breast, and names him the king among kings who conquered every direction, worshipped at Siva's shrines and struck Mount Meru with a ball, at Senthil where devotees find the path from age to age.
75.nuance: வழிவழி அருள்பெறும் அன்பினால் உனது அடிபுகழ் அடிமை: the claim on the Lord at death is hereditary service, the வழியடிமை of 34. மகமேரு செண்டு மோதின அரசருள் அதிபதி points to the story of the Pandya king who struck Meru with a ball, which is told of Murugan born as Ugra Pandya; the text gives the deed but not the name.

76.reading: The poet sets out his learning and fame as a poet: he has read the Sangam songs and books, stories and kavyas, the sixty-four arts, the truthful word of Thiruvalluvar and the proverbs, has made garlands of many rhythms, madal, parani, kovai and kalambakam, crores of prabandhas and extempore verse like a storm, and goes about as king of sweet poetry with white umbrella, titles, flags, drums and palanquin; he asks whether this pride will not be removed. The praise tells how Vishnu, unable to defeat the fierce Jalandhara, worshipped Siva with a thousand lotuses a day, and when one flower was missing offered his eye, and received the discus that cut Jalandhara's body; Murugan, son of that Mahesa, married Indra's daughter and came to rule the poet at Senthil.
76.nuance: The song is a self-portrait of a court poet and a confession that the honours (வெண்குடை, விருது, கொடி, தண்டிகை) are pride (மால் அகந்தை). Among the learning listed is திருவள்ளுவ தேவர் வாய்மை, the Kural named as a classic. In the myth, Vishnu offering his eye to make up the missing lotus is my reading of கோ அணிந்திடு செங்கண்மால் and is not certain.

77.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women, bowing at their lotus feet, breasts thrilling, large dark eyes clashing with gold earrings, sweet lisping words, hair falling, new nail-marks and sweat on the brow, and asks whether he will not give up the 'love' of these women of wealth that makes men lose their sense in the snare of Kama, whom Siva burned to ash. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, with the demons bowing their heads to Murugan's feet and begging for his grace, and names him the Kumara of Seyppathi and Senthil by the sea.
77.nuance: பொருளின் மகளிர்: women of wealth, the Kural's phrase for courtesans, and their அன்பு is the love the poet asks to give up. In the praise the defeated demons themselves ask for grace (எங்கட்கு உன் கட் க்ருபை தா), not only the gods. செய்ப்பதி, the field town, is probably Vayalur.

78.reading: A short song: the poet, bewildered by women of fragrant sandal-dressed breasts, by eye-corners they whet like weapons and by dark hair humming with bees, asks Murugan to grant him grace with joy and love. The praise names the nephew of Hari with the kadamba garland, the vel that made the sea boil, and the true guru whom the burner of the three cities worships, at Senthil.
78.nuance: மறுகிடு மருளனை: the poet names himself the bewildered one; the remedy asked is grace given with joy (இன்புற்று அன்புற்று அருள்வாயே), as if the Lord's pleasure in giving were part of the gift. திரிபுர தகனரும் வந்திக்கும் சற்குருநாதா: Siva worships his son as teacher.

79.reading: The poet speaks of women with breasts like a tusker's, whose red eye-corners hold a man until he grows weak, and calls himself one who never suspected the mind that cuts him; he asks Murugan to rule him by giving Tamil words that string together the meaning of his golden feet. The praise names Murugan who answered the gods' distress at Sura's hands and slew Sura with his vel for love of Indra, and who rebuked the lotus-born Brahma, struck him, and as Siva's true calf lisped that meaning to him, at Thiruchendur.
79.nuance: எனக்கு என்று அப்பொருள் தங்கத் தொடுக்கும் சொல் தமிழ் தந்து: the plea is for the gift of song, as in 2 and 25. In the praise, திருக் கஞ்சத்தனைக் கண்டித்து ... குட்டி and சற்சிவக் கன்று அப்பொருள் கொஞ்சிப் பகர்வோனே give the Om story without naming Om. The dense rhythm makes much of the first half uncertain.

80.reading: The poet describes the courtesans' charms from anklets to hair, their cuckoo voices welcoming whoever looks, 'come home', their bed where they seem loving, and their play with sweat and kisses, and asks whether union with them is fitting. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which Sesha, Meru, Sura and Taraka fall and the gods dance, names the face that whispered into the father's ear, and ends with Murugan embracing Valli, 'my doll, our girl', at Senthil of tall screwpine.
80.nuance: அன்புளார் போல், 'as if loving', and வாரும் வீடே, 'come home', are the two marks of the courtesan here. தாதை காதில் அங்கு ஓது is the teaching of Siva, whispered in his ear. என் பாவை வள்ளி எங்கள் மாதை sounds like the voice of Valli's own people, which suggests the praise briefly takes another speaker.

links.note: Both picture old age with speech failing, teeth gone and a staff in hand. The Naladiyar's old man still keeps his eyes on desire; in 68 the women laugh at him, and the poet turns the scene into a prayer for Murugan to come at the hour of death.
The Kural holds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking; 69 confesses a tongue put to exactly that use, poems of praise carried from one patron's door to another.

Both list the poet's genres, கோவை, உலா, மடல் and the rest. In 69 they are tools for begging at patrons' doors; in 76 they are titles of honour and the source of the poet's pride, which he asks to have removed.
Both draw Death on his buffalo with noose and club and ask Murugan to come on the peacock at that hour; 75 grounds the claim in hereditary service, 8 in the confession that he has not served.
The Kural calls the embrace of deceiving women an அணங்கு, a possessing spirit; 73 gives the deceit a literal form, the love-pellets and the charm hidden in the betel.

The Naladiyar likens the harlot's love to lamplight that goes out when the oil runs out, and her love when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 66 stages the same course with a real lamp: she takes him upstairs by lamplight (விளக்கெடுத்து), coaxes coins, strips his hands of jewels and drives him out exhausted (இளைக்க விட்டுத் துரத்துவார்).

The Naladiyar says such women would bow and dismiss even red-eyed Mal if he came with nothing in his hand to give (விடுப்பர் தங்கையால் தொழுது). 67 gives the dismissal in the woman's own words once the man is spent: 'you are finished, go today' (அற்றனை என இன்று ஓட்டு).

The Naladiyar says learning has no shore and the learner's days are few, so one should choose what is fit, like the bird drinking the milk from the water. 70 asks that before the body ages in seeking endless crores of books (நூல் அனந்த கோடி தேடி) he be given the books of knowledge in which the Lord is mingled (நீ கலந்துள ஞான நூல்). Both set limited life against unlimited books; 70 names the choice as the jnana books.

Both quote the flattery a poet gives a patron by borrowing the god's names: in 55 'you are the noble Vel' (துங்கவேள்), in 71 'Kandan for beauty' (நிறத்திற் கந்தன்), along with Kubera and Indra. 55 asks to keep those names for Murugan; 71 confesses the hunger (பெரும் பசிக்குத் தஞ்சமென்று) that drove him to give them away.

The Kural calls the petty knowledge that takes the impermanent for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்) the lowest. 72 opens with that error made personal, taking the impermanent thing for oneself (நிலையாப் பொருளை உடலாக் கருதி), and follows it with what results: wasted days, deafness, blindness and the bed of filth.

The Kural calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that true knowledge removes by seeing the true thing. 74 places the courtesans within that larger condition, the darkness of defiled birth and its bonds (பங்கமேவும் பிறப்பு அந்தகாரம் ... பந்தபாசம்), and asks for the feet as the way out.

The Kural names them பொருட்பெண்டிர், women of wealth, whose false embrace is like a hired man clasping a stranger's corpse in a dark room. 77 uses the same name, பொருளின் மகளிர், after a full description of the embrace, and asks whether he will not give up their 'love' (அன்புப் பண்பு); the description the Kural refuses, 77 gives in full before refusing it.

Both make a woman's eyes a weapon: the Kural's eyes eat the life of those who see them and are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentleness; 78's eye-corners are whetted as weapon upon weapon (படையம் படையென அந்திக்கும் கண்கடை). The Kural's lover is held in wonder; 78 names the same look the source of his bewilderment (மறுகிடு மருளன்) and asks for grace.

Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ் செய்யுமாறே). 79 asks for the same gift: Tamil words that string together the meaning of his golden feet (அப்பொருள் தங்கத் தொடுக்கும் சொல் தமிழ் தந்து). Both make Tamil verse the purpose for which the poet is given.

The Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), bring ruin. 80 gives the sweet words, the cuckoo voice saying 'come home' (வாரும் வீடே), and their show of love on the bed, 'as if loving' (அன்புளார் போல்), and asks whether union with them is fitting.

source_issues: Song 70: one corrupt character in மதனு஡டே (line 2); probably மதனூடே.
Song 72: the source lists a heading variant (திருச்செந்தூர்) in brackets; it matches the chapter's shrine.
